summary: Dantidurga overthrew the Chalukyas of Badami in 753, and his successors built an empire from the Kaveri to the Narmada, carving the Kailasa temple at Ellora and marching north to Kannauj three times in the struggle with the Palas and Pratiharas. Amoghavarsha I ruled from Manyakheta for 64 years, and Krishna III humbled the Cholas at Takkolam in 949. After Malwa's army sacked Manyakheta in 972, the vassal Tailapa II seized power in 973, and the last claimant, Indra IV, died in 982.
details: The Rashtrakutas were a family of Chalukya vassals in the northern Deccan. Their chief Dantidurga took advantage of the Chalukyas' long, draining wars with the Pallavas. In 753, according to his Samangadh copper-plate grant, he defeated the Chalukya king Kirtivarman II and took the northern Chalukya lands, the founding moment of the Rashtrakuta empire. Dantidurga died about 756 without a son, and his uncle Krishna I succeeded him, finishing the destruction of Chalukya power in the south.

Krishna I (c. 756–774) extended Rashtrakuta rule over most of present-day Karnataka and the Konkan coast. He is generally credited with the Kailasa temple at Ellora, a whole Shiva temple cut downward out of a single basalt cliff, though the inscriptions linking it to him are not certain proof. Its tower rises about 33 metres above the courtyard. It is the largest of Ellora's 34 cave temples and is seen as the peak of Indian rock-cut architecture, a statement of the new dynasty's wealth and confidence.

Krishna I's son Govinda II was pushed aside in 780 by his brother Dhruva Dharavarsha, a vigorous soldier. Dhruva expanded the kingdom to cover the land between the Kaveri river and central India. He then joined the contest for Kannauj, the old imperial city of the Ganges plain, which the Pratiharas of the west and the Palas of Bengal were fighting over. He defeated both rivals and returned with rich booty, but took no lasting territory. This three-way war is known as the Tripartite Struggle.

Dhruva's son Govinda III (793–814) first crushed a revolt by his elder brother Stambha and twelve allied kings. Around 800 he invaded the north and won the submission of the Pratihara emperor Nagabhata II, the Pala emperor Dharmapala and Chakrayudha, ruler of Kannauj; a later inscription boasts that his horses drank from Himalayan streams. He also put his brother Indra in charge of Gujarat, and the Cholas, Pandyas and Keralas paid him tribute. Under Govinda III the empire reached the height of its military power.

When Govinda III died in 814, his son Amoghavarsha I was only about fourteen. Relatives and vassals rebelled and briefly drove him from power, but with the help of his cousin Karka he regained control by 821. He then made peace with the Western Gangas through marriage alliances and fought the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi, defeating them at Vingavalli. Amoghavarsha went on to reign for about 64 years, one of the longest precisely dated reigns of any monarch.

Amoghavarsha I moved the capital to Manyakheta (modern Malkhed in Karnataka), which remained the Rashtrakuta capital until the empire's end. His court was a centre of learning. The Kavirajamarga, a work on poetics written around 850 and credited to the king or his court poet, is the earliest surviving work of Kannada literature. The mathematician Mahaviracharya dedicated his book to Amoghavarsha. A devout Jain who also supported Hindu temples, the king is sometimes called the 'Ashoka of the South' for his peaceable rule.

Arab merchants traded along India's west coast, which the Rashtrakutas controlled. An Arabic travel account dated 851, the Silsilat al-Tawarikh, associated with the merchant Sulaiman, counted the Rashtrakuta kingdom among the four principal empires of the world, and the merchant Sulaiman named its king, Amoghavarsha I, among the world's four great kings. The judgement reflected the empire's size, its large armies and its wealth from trade, and the welcome it gave foreign merchants.

Amoghavarsha I died in 878 and was succeeded by his son Krishna II, who ruled until 914. His reign was a time of setbacks. The Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi, in coastal Andhra, rose in revolt and fought the Rashtrakutas for years, and the empire shrank. There were wars also with the Pratiharas in the north and the Cholas in the south. The Rashtrakutas remained a great power, but the far-flung empire of Govinda III could not be held together without constant fighting.

Krishna II's grandson Indra III, crowned in 915, saw a chance in the family quarrels of the Pratihara rulers of Kannauj. He first drove a Pratihara vassal from Govardhana near Nasik, making the Paramaras of Malwa his own vassals, then struck deep into the Ganges–Yamuna doab. The Pratihara emperor Mahipala I fled, pursued by Indra's Chalukya vassal Narasimha, who 'bathed his horses in the Ganges'. Kannauj was destroyed and held until about 916. The raid weakened the Pratiharas for good but added no lasting territory.

Krishna III (939–967) was the last great Rashtrakuta king. In the south the Cholas of Thanjavur had grown powerful. In 948–949 Krishna, with his Western Ganga ally Butuga II, met a Chola army under the crown prince Rajaditya at Takkolam, near Kanchipuram. Rajaditya was killed, reportedly by an arrow from Butuga, and the Cholas were routed. The Rashtrakutas took the northern Chola province of Tondaimandalam, Krishna styled himself 'conqueror of Tanjore', and his armies reached Rameswaram. The empire now stretched from the Narmada to the Kaveri.

After Krishna III died in 967, his brother Khottiga came to the throne, and the vassals began to drift away. The Paramaras of Malwa, once Rashtrakuta vassals, had grown strong north of the Narmada. In 972 the Paramara king Siyaka Harsha invaded, defeated the Rashtrakuta army and plundered Manyakheta itself. The sack shattered the dynasty's prestige. Khottiga died soon afterwards, and his nephew Karka II inherited an empire whose vassals no longer feared it.

Tailapa II governed Tardavadi, in the Bijapur region, as a Rashtrakuta vassal and claimed descent from the old Chalukyas of Badami. In 973 he overthrew the weakened emperor Karka II and took the throne, founding the Western Chalukya dynasty and making Manyakheta his capital. Many former Rashtrakuta vassals, such as the Shilaharas of the Konkan, accepted him as overlord. The Rashtrakuta empire passed almost whole into the hands of the new dynasty, roughly two centuries after the Rashtrakutas had displaced the Chalukyas.

Indra IV, a member of the Rashtrakuta royal house, carried on as a claimant to the throne after 973, but he could not defeat Tailapa II. Giving up the struggle, he turned to the Jain faith of many of his ancestors. On 20 March 982 he died by sallekhana, the Jain ritual fast to death, at the hill shrine of Shravanabelagola in southern Karnataka. With him the Rashtrakuta dynasty came to an end, and the Western Chalukyas ruled the whole of its former Deccan empire.
